title: Lecture 4: Derivatives and Rates of Change
mainIdeas: A slope tells you how fast one quantity changes when another changes.
The derivative is the slope at a single point: the instantaneous rate of change.
In business, derivatives give marginal cost and show where profit peaks.

concepts.name: Slope of a straight line
concepts.explanation: The slope of a line is rise over run: how much y changes for each one-unit increase in x. A negative slope means y falls as x grows. On a straight line the slope is the same everywhere.
concepts.misconception: Reading a steeper line as a bigger number even when it falls. A line dropping fast has a large negative slope, not a large positive one.
concepts.bridge: A straight piste dropping 40 metres for every 100 metres you ski forward has slope -0.4, from the top lift to the bottom.

graph.title: A straight piste: height over distance

concepts.name: Average rate of change
concepts.explanation: The average rate of change of f between a and b is (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a). It is the slope of the straight line joining the two points, and it ignores what happens in between.
concepts.misconception: Thinking the average rate tells you the rate at every point between a and b. It hides the steep and the flat parts.
concepts.bridge: Your run drops 900 metres over 1600 metres. The average slope is the same whether the steep wall is at the top or the bottom.

concepts.name: The derivative
concepts.explanation: The derivative f'(x) is the slope of the tangent line at x: the limit of the average rate of change as the interval shrinks to zero. It is the instantaneous rate of change at one point.
concepts.misconception: Treating f'(x) as the value of the function. f(x) is the height; f'(x) is how steep it is right there.
concepts.bridge: Height is where you are on the mountain. The derivative is how steep it is under your skis right now, and it changes as you go down.

concepts.name: Power rule
concepts.explanation: For f(x) = x^n, the derivative is f'(x) = n x^(n-1). Constants drop out, and a constant factor stays in front. So 3x^2 + 5 has derivative 6x.
concepts.misconception: Lowering the power but forgetting to multiply by the old exponent, so x^3 becomes x^2 instead of 3x^2.
concepts.bridge: Ski wax sales grow like x^2 over the season: the derivative 2x says sales pick up faster every week.

graph.title: y = x² and its tangent at x = 3

concepts.name: Marginal cost
concepts.explanation: Marginal cost C'(x) is the derivative of the cost function: roughly the extra cost of producing one more unit at output level x.
concepts.misconception: Confusing marginal cost with average cost. Average cost is C(x)/x; marginal cost is the slope of C at x.
concepts.bridge: A ski-jacket maker at 100 jackets a day: marginal cost is what jacket number 101 adds to the bill.

graph.title: Cost of x ski jackets per day

concepts.name: Maximum where the derivative is zero
concepts.explanation: At the top of a smooth curve the tangent is flat, so f'(x) = 0. To find maximum profit, set P'(x) = 0 and solve, then check the slope changes from positive to negative.
concepts.misconception: Assuming every point with f'(x) = 0 is a maximum. It can also be a minimum or a flat point.
concepts.bridge: A ski rental shop: more rentals bring more profit until staff and skis run out. The top of the profit hill is where the slope is zero.
